steps.title: try / except
body: except ZeroDivisionError as e:     # catch (DivideByZeroException e)

Exceptions you will meet daily: `ValueError` (bad value: `int("x")`), `TypeError` (wrong type: `"a" + 1`), `KeyError` (missing dict key), `IndexError`, `AttributeError`, `FileNotFoundError`, `ZeroDivisionError`.

steps.explain: Each `except` is tried in order; the first matching one handles the exception.

steps.prompt: Match each line to the exception it raises.

steps.title: else and finally
body: print("parsed", value)     # only if NO exception happened
print("always runs")       # cleanup, success or failure
`else` keeps the `try` block small: only the line that can fail goes inside `try`, so you do not accidentally catch errors from the code that follows. C# has no `else` here.

steps.explain: `finally` runs even when the `try` or `except` block returns. Its output appears before the caller prints the returned value.

steps.prompt: Why is a bare `except:` (or `except Exception:` that silently passes) usually a bad idea?
options: It hides bugs, including typos like `NameError`, and even Ctrl+C for bare `except:`
steps.explain: Catch the specific exceptions you expect and can handle. Let everything else crash loudly, just as you would avoid `catch (Exception) { }` in C#.

steps.prompt: Arrange the lines to read a number, falling back to 0 on bad input, and always print `checked`.
Catch two exception types in one clause.

steps.title: Safe divide
prompt: Read lines of `a b` until `end`. For each, print `a / b` to 2 decimal places. On errors print instead:
- `not numbers` if either is not a number
- `need two values` if the line does not split into exactly two parts
At the end print `ok N, failed M`.
solution: print("need two values" if "unpack" in str(e) else "not numbers")
hints: Unpacking the wrong number of parts raises `ValueError` too; check the parts count first, or look at the message.
